params.text:
Behaviour that challenges, not “difficult people”

When someone shouts, refuses care or lashes out, it is tempting to label them as aggressive or difficult. A far more useful view is that all behaviour is a form of communication. What looks like defiance is very often distress — a person trying to tell you that something is wrong when they cannot find the words.

This matters most for people living with dementia, a learning disability or autism, who may struggle to explain what they need. Someone in pain, frightened or overwhelmed may reach for the only response they have left. The behaviour is a signal, not the whole story, and rarely a personal attack on you.

Looking for the unmet need: common causes and triggers

People rarely become distressed or aggressive without a reason. Challenging behaviour is very often an expression of an unmet need or an attempt to communicate something the person cannot put into words. Stay curious about the underlying cause rather than reacting only to the surface — understanding it helps you respond with compassion rather than confrontation.

  • Unmet needs — hunger, thirst, needing the toilet, being too hot or too cold.
  • Pain or illness — discomfort or infection that a person cannot easily describe, especially where speech is affected.
  • Fear and frustration — feeling powerless, rushed, frightened, or not listened to.
  • Dementia or confusion — disorientation, misreading a situation, or not recognising you, the room, or what is happening next.
  • Environment — noise, crowding, heat, or rushing that feels overwhelming.
  • Loss of control — having choices taken away or being hurried through personal care.
  • Communication breakdown — not being understood, sensory impairment, or language differences.
  • Unrealistic expectations — a person or relative expecting something that cannot be delivered.

When you notice and meet the need, the distress usually eases on its own — without anyone having to “win”.

params.alt: A care worker sitting with an older person they support, beside the heading “Behaviour that challenges, not “difficult people””. Key points: Unmet needs; Pain or illness; Fear and frustration.

params.question: A resident with dementia becomes agitated and pushes your hand away during personal care. What is the most helpful first way to understand this?

answers.text: As communication — she may be in pain, frightened or feeling rushed, and is telling you something is wrong.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Treating behaviour as a message about an unmet need helps you respond to the cause rather than the surface.

answers.text: As deliberate aggression that you must firmly correct.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Framing distress as defiance tends to escalate it and misses what the person actually needs.

answers.text: As a sign she is simply a difficult person to care for.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Labelling the person, rather than looking for the trigger, stops you finding what would actually help.

answers.text: As something to ignore so it does not get attention.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Ignoring distress leaves the need unmet and the person is likely to become more distressed, not less.
